name: all-2
statement: Most of the RL-Zero-Math gain is a linear accumulation of many small skill improvements: fewer arithmetic slips and misreads, better method choice, and finishing long problems. The answer format (boxing instead of the base's 'Answer:' line) is a cheap side effect that carries almost no accuracy. The improvements are many distinct, input-dependent contributions written into specific matrices, so a fraction of the delta recovers a proportional fraction of the gain: accuracy grows linearly with delta scale (a = 0.25 gives about a quarter of the gain). The cue acts through the prompt on a route separate from RL's weight change, so cue and partial delta add, and other RL runs (Code-RL) share none of the math gain.
scope: Olmo-3-1025-7B base vs Olmo-3.1-7B-RL-Zero-Math (and the Code-RL delta from the same base), MATH-500 and the 328 harder problems, plain and cued prompts, T 0.6-1.0, weight interpolation and partial copies of the delta. It claims the skill accumulation explains the whole plain-base to RL gap, including the last points past the cued-base level (long-problem finishing, fewer slips); the cue's gain on the base is a prompt effect outside RL's weight change. It does not cover pass@k.

explains.quote: All MLP from RL alone 86.4; attention + norms alone 83.0
explains.how: The MLP and attention halves each carry their own share of the improvements, and their scores differ only on cap-hit problems: long-problem finishing is a separable component written in specific matrices, as an accumulation of distinct pieces predicts, not one switch both halves flip equally.

A rescaled random sample is an unbiased estimate of the full delta, so to first order it applies the same sum of small contributions; that is exactly what a linear accumulation needs, while a top-k subset, which drops most contributions, recovers almost nothing.

explains.quote: Every arm that recovers accuracy also takes RL's format and length
explains.how: Length tracks accuracy because the added skill is longer, more careful work; the format change rides along as a side effect of the same training, carried in proportion to how much of the delta each arm holds.

explains.quote: D follows the answer format, not correctness
explains.how: The format token is where the two models differ most in log-probability, yet RL gives a wrong box the base's probability, so the format difference does not select right answers; the accuracy comes from the many small changes spread through the reasoning.
RL has removed the base's 'Answer:' line, but 121 of those 132 base answers were right anyway: the format change buys almost no accuracy.
The cue changes only how an answer opens; RL's accuracy is skill held in its weights, which two prompt tokens can neither add nor take away.

The cue works through the prompt, on a route separate from RL's weight change: it removes a plain-prompt failure of the base, while RL's weights add skill the cued base still lacks, as its 5-12 point deficit on AMC, AIME and OlympiadBench shows.

The cue token reaches the top readouts of only 13-15 of 96 late directions in either RL delta, a shared vocabulary of deliberation words, while the two deltas are nearly orthogonal as wholes: the RL runs write separate changes that happen to read out similar words.
In that pair accuracy rises steadily, nearly in proportion to lambda, from 0.1 to 0.7; the turn below full scale is the onset of breakdown (early end-of-text stops climbing), not a saturating switch.

explains.quote: closes 80-100 % of the gap on Math-500
explains.how: Label-free training on a math-specialized Qwen base reaches the easy MATH-500 gain but only 0-70 % on AIME, so the harder part of the gain is skill that must accumulate through rewarded training.

conflicts.how: Neuron contributions to KL add linearly (0.542 nats predicted, 0.549 measured), the direct signature of a gain built from many small additive contributions; accuracy follows the distribution, so it too is linear in the delta.
The Math-RL and Code-RL deltas are nearly orthogonal and agree in sign on only 50.8 % of entries, so the two runs write separate changes and Code-RL carries none of the math gain.
A cued, restarted base that already answers in the right format still trails RL by 10 points: that gap is skill the RL weights added, which no change of mode supplies.
RL avoids arithmetic slips, misreads and wrong methods that the cued base makes, exactly the small, numerous improvements the accumulation consists of.

rival: The gain is a saturating answer-mode switch: deliberate, box the answer and stop, flipped by any unbiased fraction of the delta, so accuracy is a sharply concave function of delta scale and the cue flips the same switch. Separation: the rival predicts base + 0.25*(RL - base) on the plain prompt recovers about three quarters of the gain (about 375/500 at T 1.0) and that the cue adds almost nothing at a = 0.5. This theory predicts about a quarter of the gain at a = 0.25 (about 284/500) and that the cue still adds about 90 items at a = 0.5.

predictions.experiment: base + 0.25*(RL - base), plain prompt, T 1.0 / top-p 1.0, cap 16,384, grader v3, MATH-500 one sample
base + 0.5*(RL - base), plain prompt, T 1.0 / top-p 1.0, cap 16,384, grader v3, MATH-500 one sample
base + 0.5*(RL - base) with the opening cue minus the same model with the plain prompt, T 1.0, MATH-500
predictions.refuted_by: the cue adds fewer than 40 items at a = 0.5

predictions.experiment: base + 1.0*(Code-RL - base) (Olmo-3.1-7B-RL-Zero-Code final), plain prompt, T 1.0 / top-p 1.0, grader v3, MATH-500 one sample
predictions.refuted_by: above 280 (well past the plain base's 224 plus noise) or the share of answers with an 'Answer:' line falls below 20 %
